reading_log.extent: University-hosted primary scan. Printed pp. 96–101 read (pp. 98–101 through OCR of page images); remaining essay and notes unread in this pass. English collection/date independently confirmed by Smithsonian Libraries record siris_sil_435694, https://www.si.edu/object/clues-myths-and-historical-method-carlo-ginzburg-translated-john-and-anne-c-tedeschi%3Asiris_sil_435694 . The 2013 publisher reissue is not the original date. This is the English collection version of an earlier essay, not a claim that the argument originated in 1989. Its Freud/Morelli genealogy is Ginzburg’s argument; Freud’s original text and the Morelli volumes were not independently collated. No direct quotation is newly reproduced.

Indexed institutional SBN Bologna catalogue record CFI0016674 confirms the 1986 first Italian collection, author, publisher, and earlier component essay dates, including Spie (1979). The Turin State Archive Einaudi originals/proofs inventory, printed p. 206, separately records the 1986 first edition and proof date 18 February 1986: https://archiviodistatotorino.cultura.gov.it/upload/Einaudi_Originali%20e%20bozze_unico.pdf . Metadata only for the Italian volume; direct Italian body and original 1979 essay uncollated. The selected Clues argument is read separately in the English translation of the collection (1989), not dated as newly invented in 1986 or 1989.

Official institutional full PDF. Preface pp. 5–6, Richter pp. 7–9, Pocock pp. 47–58 and Koselleck pp. 59–66 read closely; final reply pp. 67–70 consulted for concluding context. Copyright/preface date the publication to 1996; the preface dates the symposium to December 1992. Claims are dated to the published text, not assumed identical to an uncollated oral delivery. Pocock explicitly says he does not read German and responds through Richter’s presentation. His criticism of the lexicon and his particular criticism of Skinner coexist with openness to complementary methods. Koselleck argues for interdependence, not an opposition between two homogeneous schools. Other contributions and original German lexicon entries unread, except as stated. No new direct quotations.

Publisher-rendered opening text and notes read through indexed Oxford Academic rendering on 2026-10-24; direct HTML/PDF fetch was blocked (403), so this is not claimed as a complete-article reading. Opening distinguishes microhistory’s microscopic reading from small objects, and two tendencies of global history; his skepticism is directed mainly at the spatially extended tendency, not every connected history. Closing indexed paragraph corroborates agreement with Subrahmanyam. Remaining argument/body and works he cites unread in this pass. The dated event identifies the published intervention; new prose paraphrases the available opening.

Official Cambridge excerpt printed pp. 1–4 read through OCR, plus the complete preface ix–xiv and copyright leaf in publisher-supplied 2012 Canto Classics preview https://api.pageplace.de/preview/DT0400.9781107299979_A23760718/preview-9781107299979_A23760718.pdf . Copyright explicitly says first published 1998, thirteenth printing 2010, Canto edition 2012; do not substitute the Cambridge Core record’s inconsistent 1997 print-year field. The preface dates the inaugural lecture to 12 November 1997 and states the neo-Roman/liberal contrast as the author’s program; no independent validation of its historical completeness. Body after p. 4 and the full lecture unexamined. No new direct quotations.

Author’s university-repository open-access publisher PDF, https://api.repository.cam.ac.uk/server/api/core/bitstreams/e7c29e85-0de1-427d-9369-b80c241dea6b/content . Printed pp. 1–4 read closely, later discussion and endnotes consulted for the six-volume Barbarism and Religion dates (1999–2015) and its first/last volume titles. Robertson’s account is explicitly a named reader’s reconstruction, not new reading of Pocock’s books. His criticism of Pocock’s late sovereign narratives remains a reader’s judgment; those essays and the cited private correspondence were not read and no new claim from them is proposed here. No claim that this 2025 article is Pocock’s own work.

Complete six-page official Reviews in History PDF read in the web rendering: https://reviews.history.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/pdf/Reviews_in_History_-_History_in_the_Plural_An_Introduction_to_the_Work_of_Reinhart_Koselleck_-_2012_06_28.pdf . This is Dahlstrom’s account of Olsen’s account of Koselleck; Olsen’s full book and the books discussed remain unread in this pass. Supports qualified bibliography/dates for Kritik und Krise (1959), Preussen zwischen Reform und Revolution (1967) and Zeitschichten (2000), and attributed account of their arguments/reception. The 1953 dissertation date is not adopted because other existing bibliography dates the revised thesis 1954. The lexicon’s substantive completion and later index volumes are not conflated. No fresh quotation.

Institutional Luhmann archive bibliographic record confirms all three coeditors, volume, original year 1972 and publisher. Metadata only; individual entries and the original introduction unread. Koselleck’s own 1996 response, the retained Futures Past primary reading and the named scholarly accounts separately support methodological discussion. The full 1972–97 series is not dated as if it were a single volume.

limits: No complete biographies, universal method definitions or continuous careers asserted.
Ginzburg’s 1992 Just One Witness primary-access gap remains.
Levi 2019 relies on the publisher-rendered opening, not a full-article reading; criticism is limited to the tendency he specifies.
Pocock’s 1996 claims about German Begriffsgeschichte acknowledge his inability to read German; he responds through Richter.
Dahlstrom on Olsen is second-order mediation, not a fresh reading of Koselleck’s early books or Habermas’s review.
New direct quotations avoided; historic quotations in repaired edge evidence are retained verbatim.
All source PDFs and OCR are local temporary research files, outside browser exports and this packet.
